theory.intro: Simple interest is a fixed percentage of the **original deposit** every year, so the balance grows by the same amount each year and its graph is a straight line. Compound interest is a percentage of the **current balance**, so each year's interest is bigger than the last and its graph is a curve that bends upwards. To compare two offers, work out the total each one gives over the same term, then subtract.
facts: Simple interest: $I = Prn$, so the balance after $n$ years is $P + Prn$.
Compound interest: $FV = PV(1+r)^{n}$, so the interest earned is $FV - PV$.
At the same rate the two are equal after one period; from the second period on the compound account is ahead, and the gap widens every year.
A higher simple rate can beat a lower compound rate over a short term, but compound growth catches up and overtakes it if the term is long enough.
On the same axes the simple interest graph is a straight line and the compound interest graph is a curve that gets steeper.
Work out each total in one calculation and round only at the end; rounding part-way through shifts the difference by cents.
steps: Find the total from the simple interest offer.
Find the total from the compound interest offer.

foundation.question_text: $\$8000$ is invested for $4$ years at $5\%$ p.a. How much more interest does an account paying compound interest earn than an account paying simple interest, to the nearest cent?

A credit union offers $6\%$ p.a. simple interest and a bank offers $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually. $\$15\,000$ is invested with each for $3$ years. Find the difference between the two final balances, to the nearest cent.
$\$6000$ is invested for $1$ year, one account at $7\%$ p.a. simple interest and one at $7\%$ p.a. compounding annually. How much more interest does the compound account earn?
foundation.solution_text:
$I = 6000\times0.07\times1$
$=\$420$
$FV = 6000(1.07)^{1}$
$=\$6420$, so the compound interest is also $\$420$.
Difference $=420-420$
$=\$0$

foundation.question_text: $\$4000$ is invested for $2$ years at $10\%$ p.a. How much more interest does an account paying compound interest earn than an account paying simple interest?

A bank offers $4.5\%$ p.a. simple interest and a credit union offers $4.5\%$ p.a. compounding annually. $\$12\,000$ is invested with each for $5$ years. How much more interest does the credit union account earn, to the nearest cent?

The table shows the balance of two accounts, each opened with $\$9000$ at $5\%$ p.a. One pays simple interest and the other compounds annually.

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}\text{Year}&1&2&3\\\hline \text{Account M}&\$9450&\$9900&\$10\,350\\\hline \text{Account N}&\$9450&\$9922.50&\$10\,418.63\end{array}$

Which account pays compound interest? Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
Account M rises by $\$450$ every year, a constant amount.
Account N rises by $\$450$, then $\$472.50$, then $\$496.13$, a growing amount.
Account N pays compound interest, because each year's interest is calculated on the new balance and so is larger than the year before.

development.question_text: Bank A offers $7\%$ p.a. simple interest. Credit union B offers $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually. $\$9000$ is invested for $5$ years. Which gives the greater final balance, and by how much, to the nearest cent?

Bank A offers $7\%$ p.a. simple interest and credit union B offers $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually. $\$9000$ is invested for $10$ years. Which gives the greater final balance, and by how much, to the nearest cent?
development.solution_text:
Bank A: $9000+9000\times0.07\times10$
$=\$15\,300$
Credit union B: $9000(1.06)^{10}$
$=\$16\,117.63$
Difference $=16\,117.63-15\,300$
$=\$817.63$
Credit union B gives the greater balance, by $\$817.63$.

development.question_text: $\$6000$ is invested at $8\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounding annually. Find the difference between the two balances after $3$ years and after $6$ years, each to the nearest cent, and state how many times larger the second difference is, to $1$ decimal place.

The same amount is invested for $4$ years in two accounts, one at $9\%$ p.a. simple interest and one at $9\%$ p.a. compounding annually. The compound account earns $\$386.86$ more interest. Find the amount invested, to the nearest dollar.

The table shows the balance of two accounts, each opened with $\$20\,000$ at $7\%$ p.a. One pays simple interest and the other compounds annually.

$\begin{array}{c|cccc}\text{Year}&1&2&3&4\\\hline \text{Simple}&\$21\,400&\$22\,800&\$24\,200&\$25\,600\\\hline \text{Compound}&\$21\,400&\$22\,898.00&\$24\,500.86&\$26\,215.92\end{array}$

Find the difference between the two balances after year $4$, and state what is happening to the difference from year to year.
development.solution_text:
Difference after year $4$ $=26\,215.92-25\,600$
$=\$615.92$
The differences are $\$0$, $\$98$, $\$300.86$ and $\$615.92$, so the gap widens every year, because the compound account earns interest on interest already paid.

development.question_text: Offer A pays $10\%$ p.a. simple interest and Offer B pays $8\%$ p.a. compounding annually, on a deposit of $\$4000$. Find the first whole year in which Offer B is ahead of Offer A.
development.solution_text:
Offer A: $4000+400n$
Offer B: $4000(1.08)^{n}$
$n=6$: $\$6400$ and $\$6347.50$, so A is ahead.
$n=7$: $\$6800$ and $\$6855.30$, so B is ahead.
Offer B is first ahead after $7$ years.

mastery.question_text: $\$25\,000$ is invested at $6.4\%$ p.a. compounding annually for $6$ years. Find the simple interest rate that would earn the same total interest over those $6$ years, correct to $2$ decimal places.

Offer A pays $9\%$ p.a. simple interest and Offer B pays $7\%$ p.a. compounding annually, on a deposit of $\$12\,000$. Find the first whole year in which Offer B is ahead of Offer A, and how far ahead it is at that time, to the nearest cent.

$\$10\,000$ is invested at $5\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounding annually. In which year does the compound account first earn more than $\$100$ more interest in that single year than the simple account earns?
mastery.solution_text:
The simple account earns $10\,000\times0.05=\$500$ each year, so the compound account must earn more than $\$600$ in one year.
Interest in year $n$ $=10\,000(1.05)^{n-1}\times0.05$
$n=4$: $10\,000(1.05)^{3}\times0.05=\$578.81$
$n=5$: $10\,000(1.05)^{4}\times0.05=\$607.75$
The compound account first earns more than $\$100$ extra in a single year in year $5$.
